outcome: The lower bound on the length of the shortest opaque set for the unit square was improved by more than a factor of 3 (Kiderlen & Pausinger, arXiv:2509.08842, building on a stability observation of Steinerberger, arXiv:2501.01004), and a new explicit lower bound for the unit disc was derived in the same paper; the problem itself (finding the true shortest opaque forest for the square, disc, triangle, or general convex sets) remains open.
summary: Since the frozen revision (26 Jan 2024) the only substantive development on this exact problem — finding the shortest opaque set/forest for standard shapes such as the unit square, unit disc, and equilateral triangle — is a pair of connected results improving the *lower bound* on the length of such sets, which remains far short of resolving the problem. Stefan Steinerberger (arXiv:2501.01004, submitted 2 Jan 2025, published in Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2026) proved a stability version of Jones' 1962 inequality (L ≥ |∂Ω|/2), showing that if the excess length L − |∂Ω|/2 is small, an opaque set must be made of curves whose tangent directions closely track the boundary's. Markus Kiderlen and Florian Pausinger (arXiv:2509.08842, submitted 5 Sept 2025, v2 10 Dec 2025, published in Acta Mathematica Hungarica, 2026) used this stability result to sharpen the general method of Kawamura–Moriyama–Otachi–Pach, improving the explicit numerical lower bound for the unit square 'by more than a factor of 3' beyond the prior bound (previously ~2.00002 above the perimeter-halving value of 2), and derived a new explicit lower bound for the unit disc exploiting its symmetry. Neither paper touches the upper bound (the conjectured-optimal disconnected forest of length 2 + (1/2)√6 ≈ 2.639 for the square, or ≈4.7998 for the disc) nor settles any case; the square, disc, and triangle instances of the problem remain open, as does the general problem. This is squarely a bound moving on a problem that stays open, i.e. `progress`, not a resolution or even a settled case (`partial` would require an instance to close). A separate 2024–2025 preprint by Zhipeng Deng, 'A General Solution to Bellman's Lost-in-a-Forest Problem' (arXiv:2412.10686, Dec 2024, rev. June 2025), claims a general computational framework it says extends to 'the shortest opaque set problem,' but this is Bellman's lost-in-a-forest search problem (finding an escape path from an unknown forest shape), a related but distinct problem from the opaque-set/opaque-forest blocking problem; I did not find evidence its framework has produced any new bound or result specifically on opaque sets, so I treat it as a related problem rather than a case of this one and exclude it from the status-determining event. No source anywhere in this research — the two arXiv preprints, their published journal versions, the Wikipedia 'Opaque set' and 'Opaque forest problem' articles, or search results for AI/LLM involvement — mentions any AI system, machine-learning tool, or computer-assisted proof technique (SAT solvers, interval arithmetic, etc.) being used in obtaining these results; both papers are traditional human mathematical arguments. `ai_role` is therefore `none`.
competing_reading: One could argue the Kiderlen–Pausinger unit-disc bound is a genuinely new result (not merely an improvement of an existing number, since no explicit disc bound existed before) and so might be read as `partial` progress specific to that shape rather than generic `progress`. I did not adopt this reading because the disc's *true* shortest opaque set is still entirely unknown — only a weak lower bound now exists where essentially none did before — so no case of the problem was settled, only the search space narrowed, consistent with `progress`. Also, the Wikipedia article now titled 'Opaque forest problem' (as opposed to 'Opaque set') appears to be a retitling/split of the article that existed under 'Opaque set' at the frozen revision; this is an encyclopedia-structure change unrelated to mathematical progress and I did not treat it as a finding.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that the known upper-bound construction (length 2 + (1/2)√6 for the square, or the Makai disconnected barrier for the disc) is optimal, or any new construction beating those upper bounds, would move the status to `partial` (or `resolved` if it settled a full case with matching upper and lower bounds). Confirmation of what Deng's Bellman-forest framework has or has not produced for opaque sets specifically (e.g., a later paper applying it) would also be worth checking.
